claims.text: In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature plastic strain is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and sliding behavior.
In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys, high-temperature toughness is primarily governed by grain-boundary stability and sliding behavior.
Targeted thermomechanical engineering can produce more stable grain boundaries.
More stable grain boundaries suppress intergranular cracking.
Engineered grain boundaries promote controlled grain-boundary sliding and thereby enhance plastic deformation and toughness.
Without optimized grain boundaries, early intergranular failure dominates even when dislocation-mediated plasticity is active.
Targeted thermomechanical treatments can modify grain-size and grain-boundary-misorientation distributions while alloy chemistry is held constant.
At high temperatures, increased thermal motion and atomic mobility are concentrated near grain boundaries.
At high temperatures, grain-boundary sliding can play a leading role in deformation of high-entropy alloys.
Optimized stable grain boundaries delay the onset of intergranular sliding and cavitation.
Delaying intergranular sliding and cavitation improves plastic strain and toughness.
Compared with the conventional baseline, grain-boundary-engineered alloys will sustain greater plastic strain before crack initiation.
Compared with the conventional baseline, grain-boundary-engineered alloys will have higher toughness and delayed intergranular crack propagation.
Grain-boundary engineering will shift high-temperature irradiated fracture from intergranular toward transgranular modes.
At lower temperatures, deformation may shift toward dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Strain rate affects dislocation activity and may alter the relative importance of grain-boundary and dislocation mechanisms.
The relative contribution of grain-boundary and dislocation mechanisms may depend on irradiation dose.
The proposed grain-boundary-controlled regime applies at approximately 700–1200 °C under fusion-relevant irradiation.
